# Mettā Sutta (Kp 9 (PTS Kp 8))

**ID:** Kp 9 (PTS Kp 8)
**Section:** Khuddakapāṭha (kp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Mettā Sutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0501m.mul8.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mettā Sutta* (commonly known as the *Karaṇīyametta Sutta* or *Karaṇīyamettasutta*, Kp 9 / PTS Kp 8) is the ninth and concluding discourse of the *Khuddakapāṭha* [Williams & Ladwig 2012; Crosby 2014]. The discourse consists of ten four-line verses composed in the Old Āryā metre [Symposium 2013; Crosby 2014]. It outlines the foundational moral qualities of a virtuous practitioner skillful in pursuing spiritual welfare, expounds the meditative cultivation of boundless loving-kindness (*mettā*) toward all living beings, and delineates the path leading from goodwill to awakening [Symposium 2013; Crosby 2014]. Central to the sutta is the famous simile of a mother protecting her only child with her life as an exemplar of the unrestricted goodwill to be extended toward the entire cosmos [Gombrich; Crosby 2014].

In addition to serving as a fundamental guide for meditation, the sutta is one of the most widely recited canonical protective texts (*paritta*) in Theravāda Buddhist cultures [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Crosby 2014]. It is traditionally recited to dispel fears, guard against perils, and ensure peaceful sleep without bad dreams [Williams & Ladwig 2012]. The text forms an integral part of daily monastic and lay repertoires throughout Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, featuring prominently in domestic liturgies, apotropaic rites, funeral ceremonies, and contemporary diaspora temple services chanted in both Pāli and the vernacular [Williams & Ladwig 2012; Symposium 2013; Azzopardi 2010].

 Substantial text reuse is also shared with both the *Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā* and *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, as well as the later anthology *Nīti-gantha-saṅgaho Caturārakkhadīpanī* [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language alignments detected by DharmaNexus connect segments of the sutta with the Tibetan *Mahāsāhasrapramardanī* prayer (D0813) and the Sanskrit *Svastyayanagāthā* [DharmaNexus].
